Methane · oil, gas and coal supply chains

Methane abatement database

A meta-analysis of the available data for methane leaks from both oil, gas and coal supply chains, and abatement costs for different geographies.

Oil and gas only. The cost analysis covers the US oil and gas value chain, from wellhead to city gate. Methane from coal mines is not included.

The cheapest path cuts 60 to 70% in most basins, so high-rate basins stay above 0.5%

2035, no new controlsAfter the cheapest national path0.5% target

Requiring every basin to reach 0.5% on its own would cost about a year, nearly four times the national path, though it is not like for like: basins below 0.5% cut nothing, so the national rate ends at 0.55% with fewer tonnes cut. Greater Green River, Piceance, Uinta, San Joaquin, Powder River and the smaller basins with EPA reporters (taken together) still could not get there with these measures.

One assumption at a time · net cost per year

The draws vary baseline emissions, how well the measures work, their cost, gas prices, electrification costs and how many large leaks aircraft can find. The target was reachable in every draw. The central case sits at about the 23rd percentile: the median draw costs a year, because costs climb steeply when the needed cut nears what the measures can deliver. Half the draws switch off the emission-density adjustment to costs.

Not shown as a single place

Circles sit at the approximate center of each production basin; basins are geological provinces that cross state lines. Rates are the latest measured basin averages (wellhead to city gate); the other views hold them at that level on 2035 production. Pipeline routes are EIA's interstate natural gas network (status as of 2024); they show where gas moves, not where it leaks. Stations are the 713 transmission compressor stations, storage fields and LNG terminals that reported to EPA for 2023, sized by the methane their operators reported (163 kt in all); reporting covers only larger stations and listed sources, and no measured leak rate exists for individual pipelines. Pipelines and storage outside producing basins, smaller basins, areas with no EPA reporters, and Alaska with the offshore Gulf are listed beside the map. Tap or click any circle for its numbers. Coal layer: underground coal mines reporting methane to EPA under subpart FF of the Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program, reporting year 2023 (the latest EPA has published), with coal mined from MSHA; small dots are coal mine plume sites from Carbon Mapper (2020–2026) and UNEP's Methane Alert and Response System. Surface and abandoned mines do not report to EPA and are not shown. Coal is shown for context; it is not part of the natural gas leakage rate.

Oil and gas only. The fee and rule analysis covers the US oil and gas value chain, from wellhead to city gate. Methane from coal mines is not included: the Waste Emissions Charge and EPA's OOOOb/c rules apply only to oil and gas facilities.

Of the policies modeled, a fee on every measured tonne gets closest to 0.5%

Leakage rate in 2035
No fee on measured tonnesFee on every measured tonne0.5% target

The WEC's $1,500 per tonne is set in law and not indexed, so by 2035 it is worth $1,211 in 2025 dollars. Net cost is the industry's cost after the value of gas kept; fee payments are a transfer to the Treasury and are not counted in it.

Pick a rule and a fee. A rule forces its measures wherever it reaches, whatever they cost. A fee buys every remaining tonne that costs less than the fee.

A fee at the WEC's level on every measured tonne reaches about 0.52%; getting to 0.5% takes about $1,400 a tonne

Leakage rate by fee level

Three design choices shape how far a fee at the WEC's level reaches

Fee $1,211/t, 2035

Each row adds one feature of the law to a fee on every measured tonne. The bar shows how much of the needed cut each version delivers. As written, the WEC's reach depends more on what it covers than on its price, so widening coverage moves the rate further than raising the fee.

Once EPA's methane rules are in force in every state, covered sites are exempt from the charge; with the 2024 rules in place the charge adds about 31,000 tonnes of cuts on top of them. The WEC's start moved to 2034 in July 2025, Congress struck down EPA's implementing rule in March 2025, and EPA has proposed pausing the reporting the charge depends on until 2034.

What's included

Methane from oil and gas production, gathering, processing, and transmission and storage, including unburned fuel from compressor engines. Local distribution is left out, and so is coal mine methane (coal mines appear only as a map layer on the United States tab). Alaska's reinjected gas is not counted as production.

How the baseline works

Each basin's latest measured loss rate is held at today's level and applied to its 2035 production: EIA actual production from 2023 to 2025, then EIA's AEO2026 Counterfactual Baseline to 2035. Satellite rates reported against gas sold are converted to a share of gas produced. Basins without a measurement campaign use EDF's measurement-based inventory, EI-ME.

How costs work

Twenty-five measures cut emissions in sequence within 14 source categories in each of 19 basins. Costs are in 2025 dollars per metric tonne, annualized at 7%, start from today's equipment with no rules assumed, and net out the gas kept at AEO2026 2035 regional prices.

Limitations

  • Measured rates held flat. Basin rates stay at their latest measurement to 2035. Operators already cutting would lower the baseline and the cost; a 20% lower baseline cuts the cost to $1.9 billion a year.
  • Measure performance. Effectiveness comes from EPA, ICF and field studies. If every measure works 25% less well, the cost rises to $13 billion a year.
  • Plugging. Without plugging low-producing wells, the cost rises to $6.2 billion a year and many basins cannot reach the target. Plugging is costed as bringing forward a cost owners must pay eventually (the interest on $97,000 per site over 15 years, at 1.03 wells per low-producing site), plus lost profit. The worst-emitting fifth of low-producing sites are assumed to give up $1,000 a year each; at EPA's average for low-producing gas wells ($5,950) the total rises to $3.1 billion. The cheapest path plugs roughly 88,000 sites (about 91,000 wells).
  • Growth to 2035. Each basin follows its AEO2026 region, so basins in the same region add up to the region's total. That leaves the Greater Green River, Piceance, Uinta, San Juan and Powder River 57% lower by 2035, because AEO has the Rocky Mountain region falling while the DJ grows; at the regional rate instead the cost is $2.9 billion. Areas without a basin measurement have no AEO series of their own and follow the Midcontinent region (+4%); at AEO's conventional decline (−56%) the cost is $2.2 billion, and at the Lower 48 onshore rate (+15%) $2.8 billion.
  • Satellite rates. Permian, Eagle Ford and San Joaquin rates are MethaneSAT basin-boundary values (2.5%, 1.9%, 15.5%) (Williams et al. 2026, Atmospheric Chemistry and Physics); its full observation-domain values for the Permian and Eagle Ford (2.6%, 2.4%) give $2.8 billion. Bakken, Arkoma and Barnett rest on one aircraft flight each; San Juan on 2018–20 satellite data.
  • EPA inventory by basin. EPA does not publish its inventory by basin. The page allocates EPA's 2020 gridded inventory to basins by the counties where GHGRP reporters operate, trends it to 2023 and scales it to EPA's 2023 national totals. It sets the mix of sources within each basin and the cost rescaling, not the basin total.
  • Site counts held at 2023. Costs that are per site (surveys, monitors, plugging) do not grow with production.
  • Electricity price. Electrified compression assumes 7.5 cents per kWh, below the 2025 US industrial average of about 8.5 cents. At 8.5 cents the national cost is unchanged and the basin-by-basin standard costs about 9% more.
  • Overlap between EI-ME and basin studies. To avoid counting the same methane twice, 346,000 t of EI-ME methane in counties inside measured basins is removed from the unmeasured areas, using EPA's basin-county table. The studies' production totals match those basins for most rows, but the edges are uncertain both ways: about 119,000 t in New York and the southern fringe of Appalachia may lie outside the Appalachian study area (restoring it gives $2.8 billion), and 109,000 t in the Bend Arch next to the Barnett may lie inside it (removing it gives $2.6 billion).
  • Production basis. San Juan, Powder River and the smaller basins use production reported by GHGRP reporters only, which affects the basin-by-basin standard, not the national path.
  • Reported emissions under the WEC. How much of a fixed leak shows up in a company's reported emissions is an assumption, set lower for large leaks and higher for sources EPA's reporting rule estimates with factors.
  • Rules mapped to measures. The share of each measure that EPA's rules force is an assessment of the rule text, shown in the workbook. "As finalized, 2024" does not reflect EPA's April 2026 amendments (temporary flaring, heating value).
  • No market effects. Gas prices and production do not respond to the cost of controls or to a fee.
  • Collection method. Records were collected with the use of AI and authors, checking second sources when available.
